explanations.explanation: Paul puts it plainly: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Love is the one doing the building. Knowledge is not a bad thing, but it can swell your head like dough with too much air in it. Love is what actually makes something solid.
Close, but Paul gives knowledge a different job. He says knowledge puffs up. Love is the one that builds up. I wear a very tall hat, so believe me, I know a little something about looking puffed up.

Paul does name one that builds up, and it's love. Knowledge is the one that puffs up. So he isn't saying both are empty, he's saying they do two very different things. Only one of them is building, and it's love.

explanations.answer: That person is known by God
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Paul says: "But the one who loves God is known by God." Notice he doesn't brag about what the person knows. He talks about who knows the person. Being known by God is bigger than any pile of facts in your head.

explanations.answer: That person is made wise by God
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but Paul doesn't use the word wise here. He says the one who loves God is known by God. The point is God knowing us, not us stacking up smarts. I'd take that over a bakery full of trophies.

explanations.answer: That person is given every answer
explanations.explanation: Paul never promises a full answer key. Right before this he says the one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know. What he says about the one who loves God is that this person is known by God. That's a better deal than every answer anyway.

The verse doesn't say that. Paul writes, "We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one." Nothing at all is a pretty strong way to put it. It's a lot of fuss over something the verse calls nothing at all.

Right, the verse says, "We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world…" It adds that there is no God but one (1 Corinthians 8:4). So False is the pick, however fancy the idol looks. A statue can have the best paint job in town and still be nothing at all in the world.

Paul says, "…there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." One God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. Many things in the world get called lords, but Paul names only one Lord for us. That's a short list, and I love it.

Moses is a giant in the Bible, but Paul doesn't name him here. He names Jesus Christ as the one Lord. Paul says all things came through Him and we exist through Him. Some names are famous, and one is Lord.

Elijah, a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 18:36), is a great name, but Paul doesn't put him here. The one Lord he names is Jesus Christ. He says all things came through Him and we exist through Him. Elijah isn't in this verse at all.

Paul says there is "…one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." All things came from the Father, and all things came through Jesus Christ. Same all things, both of them in the picture. That's a lot of things, and I've got a bakery to run.

Paul actually says it outright. He writes that there is "…one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." So all things came through Jesus Christ. Easy one to second-guess, but the verse is clear.

explanations.answer: As if it were sacrificed to an idol
explanations.explanation: Paul says some people "…are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol." For them it still feels tied to the idol. Their habits haven't caught up with what others know. Paul adds that since their conscience is weak, it is defiled.

explanations.answer: As if it were nothing at all
explanations.explanation: That's how the ones with knowledge see an idol, since Paul says an idol is nothing at all in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4). But these folks aren't there yet. Paul says they are still so accustomed to idols that they eat the food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. Same food, very different feeling.

explanations.answer: As if it were a holy offering
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says they eat it "…as if it were sacrificed to an idol." It's the idol they're still stuck on, not some holy offering. Holy is not the word in this verse.
Paul says the opposite. He says that since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. Weak, not strong. They're still so accustomed to idols that they eat the food as if it were sacrificed to an idol.

Right, Paul calls their conscience weak. He says they are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. Weak is the word, and he doesn't soften it.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "…food does not bring us closer to God…" Eating it earns you nothing, and skipping it costs you nothing. I've baked a LOT of cookies, and I can tell you none of them ever moved anybody closer to God.
Yes. Paul says, "But food does not bring us closer to God…" He adds that we are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. So the plate is not where the nearness to God happens.

He does. Paul writes, "Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak." Having freedom is one thing. Watching where you swing it is another. I once swung my mustache around a crowded counter, and let's just say the cookie cutters learned to duck.

Paul says exactly this. He writes, "Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak." The warning is for the well-informed believers. Their freedom is real, but it can trip someone else.

Paul asks the opposite. He says that if someone with a weak conscience sees you eating in an idol's temple, "…will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?" So the one watching is pushed toward eating, not away from it. That's the stumbling block he's warning about.

Right. Paul asks, "…will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?" The one with a weak conscience sees you eating and is encouraged to eat too. That's the danger. Watching a friend can nudge somebody the wrong direction.

Paul says it straight: "…this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge." The knowledge itself is not the problem. It's what happens when it's used without love. Remember, love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1). This is a heavy part.

Paul already said an idol is nothing at all in the world. So the idol is not what destroys this brother. He says the weak brother "…is destroyed by your knowledge." The danger comes from the well-informed one, not from the idol.

explanations.answer: The priests who serve the idol
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any priests in this passage. He says the weak brother is destroyed by the knowledge of the well-informed. That's the part that stings. It points back at the believers, not at anyone outside.

Paul says, "…you sin against Christ." He also calls the weak brother one "…for whom Christ died…" So wounding a weak conscience is not only a squabble between two people. Paul says it is sinning against Christ.

Paul doesn't mention the law here. He says that by sinning against your brothers and wounding their weak conscience, "…you sin against Christ." He also calls the weak brother one for whom Christ died. The word he uses is Christ, not the law.

You might think the damage would stay with you, but Paul says otherwise. He says that by sinning against your brothers and wounding their weak conscience, "…you sin against Christ." The weak brother is the one for whom Christ died. That's where Paul puts the weight.

Paul says, "…I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble." That's him giving up something he has every right to eat. He doesn't ask the brother to change first. I'd call that love building up.

Paul doesn't say anything about eating in private. He says, "…I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble." It's a bigger step than hiding. He's willing to give it up completely.

Paul doesn't say he'd explain it again, though that sounds like a teacher's instinct, and I'd probably say it too. What he says is, "…I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble." He chooses to give something up. That's the whole point of the lesson.
